extracted.intended_audience: high school students (ACT test-takers), parents, and educators
extracted.subtask_description: Scoring and evaluation standards for the ACT Writing Test (essay), including the analytic rubric's four domains, scoring procedures for paper and online administrations, and task expectations for essay responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject-level writing score (2–12)
rubrics_metrics.description: You will receive a total of five scores for this test: a single subject-level writing score reported on a range of 2-12, and four domain scores, also 2-12. The subject-level score will be the rounded average of the four domain scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Taking the writing test does not affect your subject area scores or your Composite score. When you have a writing test score as well as English and reading scores, an English Language Arts (ELA) score will be reported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas and Analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Scores in this domain reflect the ability to generate productive ideas and engage critically with multiple perspectives on the given issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competent writers understand the issue they are invited to address, the purpose for writing, and the audience. They generate ideas that are relevant to the situation. (This domain evaluates critical engagement with perspectives and the productivity/relevance of ideas.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Development and Support
rubrics_metrics.description: Scores in this domain reflect the ability to discuss ideas, offer rationale, and bolster an argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competent writers explain and explore their ideas, discuss implications, and illustrate through examples. They help the reader understand their thinking about the issue. (This domain centers on explanation, exploration, implications, and use of examples to support claims.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Organization
rubrics_metrics.description: Scores in this domain reflect the ability to organize ideas with clarity and purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizational choices are integral to effective writing. Competent writers arrange their essay in a way that clearly shows the relationship between ideas, and they guide the reader through their discussion. (This domain focuses on arrangement, clarity of relationships, and reader guidance.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Language Use and Conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Scores in this domain reflect the ability to use written language to convey arguments with clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competent writers make use of the conventions of grammar, syntax, word usage, and mechanics. They are also aware of their audience and adjust the style and tone of their writing to communicate effectively. (This domain assesses clarity, conventions, and appropriate register.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Task requirement: State perspective and analyze relationship to at least one other perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: Your essay will be evaluated based on the evidence that it provides of your ability to clearly state your own perspective on an issue and analyze the relationship between your perspective and at least one other perspective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The prompt asks you to generate an essay that establishes your own perspective on a given issue and analyzes the relationship between your perspective and at least one other perspective. Responses are scored using the analytic rubric across the four domains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scoring procedure — Paper testing (human raters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two trained readers will score your essay on a scale of 1-6 in each of the four writing domains. Each domain score represents the sum of the two readers' scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the readers' ratings disagree by more than one point, a third reader will evaluate the essay and resolve the discrepancy. (Domain sums therefore range 2–12; subject-level score is the rounded average of the four domain scores.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Scoring procedure — Online testing (automated scoring and human review)
rubrics_metrics.description: Essays are reviewed by an automated scoring engine trained by reference to tens of thousands of human-scored essays to ensure alignment to the ACT Writing Rubric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the engine assigns a “high confidence” rating, it will provide a single 2–12 score for each domain. If the engine cannot assign a “high confidence” rating, the essay is sent for human review. Additionally, a randomly selected sample of essays — including those rated as “high confidence” — are automatically routed for human review as part of quality assurance. Note: some state/district contracts and International ACT tests continue to use one reader paired with CRASE when scoring online.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytic scoring rubric structure
rubrics_metrics.description: The analytic scoring rubric breaks the central elements of written argument into four domains: Ideas and Analysis, Development and Support, Organization, and Language Use and Conventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As you review these domains, think about the role each plays in a written argument that accomplishes its purpose. The rubric provides standards by which essays are evaluated and helps writers understand the dimensions of writing the assessment evaluates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sample essays and exemplars
rubrics_metrics.description: ACT provides one sample prompt and six possible responses, ranging from weak to strong, to illustrate what kinds of responses score the highest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These sample essays give test-takers an idea of how to achieve their best score by showing how essays of varying quality map to rubric ratings across the domains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benchmark: average writing test score
rubrics_metrics.description: The average writing test score is between 6–7.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statistic can serve as a reference point for typical performance; individual institutions may have different expectations for acceptable or competitive scores.
